```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

health_cols <- c(Good = "#2E7D32", Fair = "#F9A825", Poor = "#C62828")
accent_green <- "#2E7D32"
accent_blue <- "#315E7D"
muted_grey <- "#9AA5B1"

class_distribution <- read_csv(
  "eda_outputs/tables/class_distribution.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
problem_health <- read_csv(
  "eda_outputs/tables/health_by_problem_count.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
species_poor <- read_csv(
  "eda_outputs/tables/poor_share_by_species.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
comparison <- read_csv(
  "results/model_comparison.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
baseline_metrics <- read_csv(
  "results/majority_baseline_metrics.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
test_metrics <- read_csv(
  "results/final_test_metrics.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
final_confusion <- read_csv(
  "results/final_confusion_matrix.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
importance <- read_csv(
  "results/final_xgboost_importance.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

metric_value <- function(metric, class_name = NA_character_) {
  result <- test_metrics |>
    filter(.metric == metric)
  if (is.na(class_name)) {
    result <- result |> filter(is.na(class))
  } else {
    result <- result |> filter(class == class_name)
  }
  result$estimate[[1]]
}

macro_f1 <- metric_value("macro_f_meas")
balanced_accuracy <- metric_value("bal_accuracy")
poor_recall <- metric_value("recall", "Poor")
poor_precision <- metric_value("precision", "Poor")

xgb_natural_checkpoint <- readRDS(
  "results/checkpoints/xgboost_natural_checkpoint.rds"
)
xgb_downsampled_checkpoint <- readRDS(
  "results/checkpoints/xgboost_downsampled_checkpoint.rds"
)

cv_metric_value <- function(checkpoint, metric, class_name = NA_character_) {
  result <- checkpoint$selected_metrics |>
    filter(.metric == metric)
  if (is.na(class_name)) {
    result <- result |> filter(is.na(class))
  } else {
    result <- result |> filter(class == class_name)
  }
  result$mean[[1]]
}

xgb_natural_macro <- cv_metric_value(
  xgb_natural_checkpoint, "macro_f_meas"
)
xgb_rebalanced_macro <- cv_metric_value(
  xgb_downsampled_checkpoint, "macro_f_meas"
)
xgb_natural_poor_recall <- cv_metric_value(
  xgb_natural_checkpoint, "recall", "Poor"
)
xgb_rebalanced_poor_recall <- cv_metric_value(
  xgb_downsampled_checkpoint, "recall", "Poor"
)
xgb_natural_accuracy <- cv_metric_value(
  xgb_natural_checkpoint, "accuracy"
)
xgb_rebalanced_accuracy <- cv_metric_value(
  xgb_downsampled_checkpoint, "accuracy"
)
xgb_selected_parameters <- xgb_downsampled_checkpoint$best_params

theme_slide <- function(base_size = 25) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_blank(),
      plot.subtitle = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      axis.title = element_text(colour = "#334E3B"),
      axis.text = element_text(colour = "#344054"),
      legend.position = "none",
      plot.margin = margin(8, 20, 8, 12)
    )
}
```

## Motivation : why investigate street-tree health? {.transition-slide}

::: {.notes}
We begin with why this classification problem matters and the decision that
the model is intended to support.
:::

## Street trees are valuable—but inspection capacity is limited

::: {.impact-grid}
::: {.impact-card}
<span class="card-icon">🌳</span>

Hundreds of thousands of trees line NYC streets
:::

::: {.impact-card}
<span class="card-icon">🔎</span>

Some require inspection or maintenance
:::

::: {.impact-card}
<span class="card-icon">⏱</span>

Professional inspection of every tree takes time
:::
:::

::: {.question-box}
Can routinely collected data help identify trees needing attention?
:::

::: {.notes}
New York City manages a very large street-tree population. Some trees need
attention, but inspecting every tree immediately is resource-intensive. Our
question is whether information already collected in the census can support
prioritisation.
:::

## Can observable characteristics classify perceived tree health?

::: {.research-question}
Can tree characteristics, site conditions and geographic information classify
living street trees as **Good**, **Fair**, or **Poor** health?
:::

::: {.class-row}
<span class="class-pill good">Good</span>
<span class="class-pill fair">Fair</span>
<span class="class-pill poor">Poor</span>
:::

::: {.goal-box}
**Goal:** a screening tool to support prioritisation—not replace professional inspection.
:::

::: {.notes}
The outcome is the census worker's perceived health rating. We frame this as a
three-class prediction problem. The model is intended as a screening aid, not
an arboricultural diagnosis and not evidence of causal effects.
:::

## The census provides scale and varied predictive signals

::: {.number-grid}
::: {.number-card}
<span class="big-number">683,788</span>

original records
:::

::: {.number-card}
<span class="big-number">652,172</span>

living trees modelled
:::

::: {.number-card}
<span class="big-number">18</span>

main predictors
:::
:::

::: {.predictor-row}
<span>🌿 **Tree**<br>species, diameter</span>
<span>🏙 **Site**<br>sidewalk, guards, stewardship</span>
<span>🩺 **Condition**<br>root, trunk, branch problems</span>
<span>📍 **Location**<br>borough, coordinates</span>
:::

<div class="source">Source: NYC Parks 2015 Street Tree Census. Health is available for living trees.</div>

::: {.notes}
The original census contains about 684 thousand records. After restricting to
living trees with a recorded health outcome, 652,172 remained. We retained 18
predictors covering the tree, its site and condition, and location.
:::

## Univariate analysis : which variables distinguish tree health? {.transition-slide}

::: {.notes}
We first ask which individual recorded characteristics show visibly different
health patterns. We focus on the strongest examples rather than every EDA plot.
:::

## More recorded problems coincide with poorer health

```{r}
#| label: plot-problem-health-presentation
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.25
#| out-width: 79%
#| fig-align: center

problem_health |>
  filter(health == "Poor") |>
  mutate(problem_group = factor(problem_group, levels = c("0", "1", "2", "3+"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(problem_group, proportion, group = 1)) +
  geom_col(fill = health_cols[["Poor"]], width = 0.62, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = percent(proportion, accuracy = 0.1)),
    vjust = -0.28,
    size = 7.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(),
    limits = c(0, 0.135),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Number of recorded root, trunk and branch problems",
    y = "Poor-health share"
  ) +
  theme_slide(26)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Poor health rises from **3.6%** with no recorded problem to **11.7%** with 3+ problems.
:::

::: {.notes}
The recorded problem indicators provide a strong signal. The Poor-health share
is about three times higher among trees with at least three recorded problems.
This is an association and may also reflect age, location, or observer effects.
:::

## Health patterns also differ substantially by species

```{r}
#| label: plot-species-presentation
#| fig-width: 11.2
#| fig-height: 4.75
#| out-width: 84%
#| fig-align: center

species_poor |>
  slice_max(proportion, n = 7, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(spc_common = reorder(spc_common, proportion)) |>
  ggplot(aes(proportion, spc_common)) +
  geom_col(fill = health_cols[["Poor"]], width = 0.7, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = percent(proportion, accuracy = 0.1)),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 6.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(),
    limits = c(0, 0.125),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Observed Poor-health share", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(24)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Multiple interacting characteristics—not one variable alone—appear relevant.
:::

::: {.notes}
Species also matters. Among common species, the Poor share reaches 11.1 percent
for Norway maples, compared with 4.1 percent overall. Together with diameter,
condition, and location patterns, this motivates models that can represent
non-linear interactions.
:::

## Machine learning : sample splits and model construction {.transition-slide}

::: {.notes}
The exploratory patterns suggest useful predictive information. We now move
from description to a leakage-safe machine-learning comparison.
:::

## Nearby trees were kept together—and the test set stayed untouched

::::: {.columns .prep-layout}
:::: {.column width="42%" .pipeline-vertical}
<div class="pipe-card"><strong>652,172</strong><br>eligible trees</div>
<div class="pipe-card development"><strong>521,746</strong><br>80% development</div>
<div class="pipe-card test"><strong>130,426</strong><br>20% final test</div>
::::

:::: {.column width="55%" .prep-steps}
::: {.prep-step}
**1. Keep nearby trees together**

Same street block stays in one partition
:::

::: {.prep-step}
**2. Handle categories consistently**

Rare and unseen levels remain valid
:::

::: {.prep-step}
**3. Reduce diameter skew**

Apply the transformation inside training
:::
::::
:::::

::: {.notes}
To reduce overly optimistic validation, trees from the same street block were
kept together. We reserved 20 percent as a final test set and did not inspect
it during model choice. Imputation, category handling, and transformation were
estimated inside the training process.
:::

## We compared simple-to-flexible models on the same evidence

::: {.model-row}
<span>Logistic<br><small>linear benchmark</small></span>
<span>Naive Bayes<br><small>probabilistic benchmark</small></span>
<span>Decision Tree<br><small>interpretable rules</small></span>
<span>Random Forest<br><small>many trees</small></span>
<span class="winner-model">XGBoost<br><small>sequential trees</small></span>
:::

::: {.refinement-flow}
<span>Prepare features</span><b>→</b><span>Compare natural vs rebalanced training</span><b>→</b><span>Refine settings with grouped CV</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
We compared five models from simple benchmarks to flexible tree ensembles. For
fair comparison they used the same predictors and resampling structure. We
also compared natural class frequencies with rebalanced training and tuned
each model using the development data only.
:::

## Better optimization : rebalancing the training procedure {.transition-slide}

::: {.notes}
The strong class imbalance means that fitting the models is not enough. We now
show how the evaluation target and rebalanced training changed model behaviour.
:::

## Accuracy alone was not enough

```{r}
#| label: plot-class-distribution-presentation
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 3.8
#| out-width: 72%
#| fig-align: center

class_distribution |>
  mutate(health = factor(health, levels = c("Good", "Fair", "Poor"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(health, proportion, fill = health)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.66) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = percent(proportion, accuracy = 0.1)),
    vjust = -0.25,
    size = 8,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = health_cols) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(),
    limits = c(0, 0.9),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.03))
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Share of living trees") +
  theme_slide(27)
```

<div class="takeaway accuracy-warning">An always-<strong>Good</strong> prediction is 81.1% accurate—so accuracy alone is misleading.</div>

::: {.macro-bridge}
We therefore selected models with **Macro-F1**, giving Good, Fair and Poor equal importance.
:::

::: {.notes}
Good accounts for 81.1 percent of living trees, while only 4.1 percent are
Poor. Accuracy would reward the majority class too heavily, so we selected
models by grouped-CV Macro-F1, which gives every class equal importance.
:::

## Rebalancing made Poor-tree screening far more sensitive

<div class="improvement-grid">
<div class="improvement-card">
<span class="improvement-label">Poor recall</span>
<span class="before-value">`r percent(xgb_natural_poor_recall, accuracy = 0.1)`</span>
<span class="change-arrow">→</span>
<span class="after-value">`r percent(xgb_rebalanced_poor_recall, accuracy = 0.1)`</span>
<small>+`r number(100 * (xgb_rebalanced_poor_recall - xgb_natural_poor_recall), accuracy = 0.1)` percentage points</small>
</div>
<div class="improvement-card">
<span class="improvement-label">Macro-F1</span>
<span class="before-value">`r number(xgb_natural_macro, accuracy = 0.001)`</span>
<span class="change-arrow">→</span>
<span class="after-value">`r number(xgb_rebalanced_macro, accuracy = 0.001)`</span>
<small>improved across the three classes</small>
</div>
<div class="improvement-card tradeoff-card">
<span class="improvement-label">Accuracy</span>
<span class="before-value">`r percent(xgb_natural_accuracy, accuracy = 0.1)`</span>
<span class="change-arrow">→</span>
<span class="after-value">`r percent(xgb_rebalanced_accuracy, accuracy = 0.1)`</span>
<small>expected trade-off for minority detection</small>
</div>
</div>

::: {.tuning-strip}
**Grouped 5-fold CV selected:** `r xgb_selected_parameters$trees` trees · depth `r xgb_selected_parameters$tree_depth` · minimum node size `r xgb_selected_parameters$min_n` · learning rate `r number(xgb_selected_parameters$learn_rate, accuracy = 0.001)`
:::

::: {.improvement-takeaway}
Rebalancing—not accuracy maximisation—made the model useful as a screening tool.
:::

::: {.notes}
This comparison isolates an important modelling improvement. With natural
class frequencies, tuned XGBoost retained high accuracy but detected only 5.2
percent of Poor trees. Rebalanced training increased Poor recall to 52.9
percent and slightly increased Macro-F1, although overall accuracy fell. We
accepted that trade-off because the project is about screening uncommon Poor
trees. The displayed hyperparameters were chosen with grouped five-fold
cross-validation before opening the final test set.
:::

## Evaluation : how does our model perform? {.transition-slide}

::: {.notes}
We now compare the candidate models, then evaluate the selected model on the
untouched test set and examine what drove its predictions.
:::

## XGBoost narrowly led the cross-validation comparison

```{r}
#| label: plot-model-comparison-presentation
#| fig-width: 11.8
#| fig-height: 4.75
#| out-width: 86%
#| fig-align: center

baseline_macro <- baseline_metrics |>
  filter(.metric == "macro_f_meas") |>
  transmute(
    model = "Always-Good baseline",
    macro_f1 = mean,
    macro_f1_std_err = std_err
  )

comparison_plot <- comparison |>
  select(model, macro_f1, macro_f1_std_err) |>
  bind_rows(baseline_macro) |>
  mutate(
    model = factor(model, levels = rev(c(comparison$model, "Always-Good baseline"))),
    highlight = case_when(
      model == "XGBoost" ~ "Winner",
      model == "Always-Good baseline" ~ "Baseline",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    )
  )

ggplot(comparison_plot, aes(macro_f1, model, fill = highlight)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.67) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = macro_f1 - macro_f1_std_err,
      xend = macro_f1 + macro_f1_std_err,
      yend = model
    ),
    colour = "#172B1C",
    linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = number(macro_f1, accuracy = 0.001)),
    hjust = -0.12,
    size = 5.8,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Winner = accent_green, Other = accent_blue,
                               Baseline = muted_grey)) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 0.42),
    breaks = seq(0, 0.4, 0.1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.01))
  ) +
  labs(x = "Mean grouped-CV Macro-F1", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(23)
```

::: {.takeaway}
XGBoost (0.378) and Random Forest (0.377) were effectively very close.
:::

::: {.notes}
XGBoost achieved the highest mean cross-validated Macro-F1, using rebalanced
training data. Its advantage over Random Forest was only about 0.0014, so we
should describe it as a narrow lead rather than a decisive victory. The model
was selected before the final test set was opened.
:::

```{r}
#| label: plot-final-confusion-presentation
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 4.7
#| out-width: 92%
#| fig-align: center

final_confusion |>
  mutate(
    truth = factor(truth, levels = c("Poor", "Fair", "Good")),
    estimate = factor(estimate, levels = c("Good", "Fair", "Poor")),
    tile_label = paste0(comma(n), "\n", percent(row_proportion, accuracy = 0.1))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(estimate, truth, fill = row_proportion)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = tile_label), size = 6.7, lineheight = 1.05) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F2F7F2", high = "#2B6A3C") +
  labs(x = "Predicted health", y = "Observed health") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 21) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "#344054"),
    plot.margin = margin(2, 8, 2, 2)
  )
```
::::
:::::

<div class="caution">Screening sensitivity came with false alarms: Poor-class precision was `r percent(poor_precision, accuracy = 0.1)`.</div>

::: {.notes}
On the untouched test set, performance closely matched cross-validation. The
model found 54.9 percent of genuinely Poor trees, but only about one in ten
Poor predictions was correct. That trade-off may be acceptable for an initial
screen, but it means predicted Poor trees still require professional review.
:::

## Location and tree size carried most predictive signal

```{r}
#| label: plot-importance-presentation
#| fig-width: 10.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: 76%
#| fig-align: center

friendly_names <- c(
  longitude = "Longitude",
  latitude = "Latitude",
  tree_dbh = "Tree diameter",
  brch_other_Yes = "Other branch problem",
  spc_common_Norway.maple = "Norway maple",
  trnk_other_Yes = "Other trunk problem",
  spc_common_honeylocust = "Honeylocust",
  sidewalk_NoDamage = "No sidewalk damage"
)

importance |>
  slice_max(Gain, n = 8, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(
    feature = recode(Feature, !!!friendly_names),
    feature = reorder(feature, Gain)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(Gain, feature)) +
  geom_col(fill = accent_blue, width = 0.68) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Share of XGBoost importance", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(21)
```

::: {.location-caveat}
Location importance may limit transfer to another city or year.
:::

<div class="source">Importance is predictive—not directional or causal.</div>

::: {.notes}
Location, diameter, condition indicators, and species contributed most to the
selected model. Importance does not tell us whether a feature improves or
worsens health, and it is not causal. Strong location importance also warns
that the 2015 NYC model may not transfer directly to another place or period.
The practical conclusion is targeted screening followed by human inspection.
:::
